before: In a separate family-alignment analysis, the mean proportion of top-five records sharing the query’s recorded catalyst family increased from 40.0% to 95.0% for iridium, 42.7% to 90.7% for organic dyes, 77.3% to 94.7% for ruthenium, 87.1% to 98.6% for TiO2, and 45.0% to 60.0% for ZnO (Figure 3c); the corresponding query counts were 8, 15, 15, 14 and 4. The effect was therefore not uniform across families, but the ranking more often retained the chemistry descriptors requested by the plan. Because catalyst-family metadata contribute to the score, this measures alignment with those descriptors, not independent proof that reaction times or yields transfer between systems. Retrieved records remain evidence for council assessment rather than ready-made operating instructions. Figure 3d illustrates the ranking change.

before: The underlying examples illustrate why these defects matter chemically and operationally. A one-shot hydrogenolysis procedure placed a vented gas–liquid separator before its only pressure-defining BPR while describing pressurized reaction, leaving the proposed gas contact and pressure boundary incompatible as written. Another mixed an empty-bed time with a different reported residence-time value, obscuring the exposure assigned to the substrate. FlowPilot was not defect-free: one CuAAC output placed Cu/C in the liquid preparation despite specifying a packed catalyst bed, a contradiction that changes how the catalyst is contacted and retained. Moreover, one judge incorrectly treated equal-reference sccm and mL min−1 values as differing by a factor of 1,000. The archived counts retain that false positive, and multiple flags can refer to one underlying defect. They are therefore reported as judge findings, not as independently confirmed physical errors or safety probabilities.

before: We implemented this arrangement using a 2 or 5 mL PFA coil in a Vapourtec UV-150 module followed by a separately illuminated 20 mL FEP coil, both at 25 ± 1 °C. The reactor–light pairing preserved the compatibility of the first-stage module while allowing the second coil to use its own irradiation source. A 2.0 mL sample loop introduced substrate 1a (0.100 M), acrylonitrile (0.200 M) and iridium photocatalyst (0.500 mM) into the carrier stream at 0.020 mL min−1. The first-stage nominal liquid times were consequently 100 and 250 min. Pure oxygen entered at the interstage mixer at a controller setting of 0.090 mL min−1. Under the proposal’s STP convention (273.15 K, 1 atm), this corresponds to 0.00402 mmol min−1 of oxygen, or 2.01 equivalents against the nominal substrate feed. The displayed second-stage index of 181.82 min uses inlet-reference gas volume, 20/(0.020 + 0.090); it is not the residence time at reactor pressure. ESI Section 8 distinguishes these nominal calculations from the experimental gas-reference and sample-collection metadata.

before: Implementation revealed an additional constraint that stoichiometry alone did not capture. An initial trial with pure oxygen at 0.43 mL min−1 and liquid at 0.020 mL min−1 showed gas backflow toward the first reactor. We specified pure oxygen in the revised design inputs and reduced the gas setting to 0.090 mL min−1; the gas choice was researcher-directed, not an autonomous discovery by the model. The proposal included a gas-line check valve, although that component alone does not establish protection of the upstream liquid branch. With a 7 bar cartridge BPR and recorded system pressures of 5.1–5.6 bar, the implemented 2 mL first-stage configuration, reported jointly for Sets 1/3, gave 97% yield, whereas the 5 mL configuration associated with Set 2 gave 98%. These are NMR yields, compared contextually with the published flow yield of 90%.57 Both operating points supported the connected transformation; the one-percentage-point difference does not resolve a residence-time benefit without replicates. Table S15 and Figures S18–S19 document the conditions, irradiation and apparatus. The case demonstrates why spatial reaction design, quantitative gas delivery and observations from the assembled apparatus must be considered together.

before: We implemented separate activation and amine feeds using two channels of the same Vapourtec E-series system, with direct interstage mixing and no intermediate isolation. Feed A contained acid (0.500 M), DPDTC (0.525 M) and DMAP (0.0500 M) in 2-MeTHF; Feed B contained benzylamine (2.10 M). For Set 1, liquid rates of 0.160 and 0.0400 mL min−1 delivered nominal acid and amine molar flows of 0.0800 and 0.0840 mmol min−1, preserving 1.05 equivalents of amine. Two 5 mL ETFE coils gave nominal times of 31.25 and 25.00 min, because the downstream coil receives both liquid feeds. This distinction is central to the design: specifying two reactor times without updating the downstream material balance would not preserve the proposed stoichiometry and exposure. The implementation used a 2.0 mL sample loop for Feed A, a 95 °C water bath for both coils and a 7 bar cartridge BPR; recorded pressure for Set 1 was 5.2–5.3 bar.

before: Set 1 gave 86% yield. Sets 2/3 shared a second implemented configuration: a 10 mL first coil and a 5 mL second coil, with feed rates of 0.280 and 0.0700 mL min−1, stage times of 35.71 and 14.29 min, and 68% yield. Both outcomes and the 98% literature batch reference are NMR yields.58 The second configuration increased nominal substrate delivery from 0.0800 to 0.140 mmol min−1 and reduced total nominal time from 56.25 to 50.00 min, but redistributed exposure toward the activation stage and away from amidation. The lower yield at this operating point, despite its longer nominal first-stage time, shows that neither upstream exposure nor total nominal time alone explains the outcome. The observations motivate further examination of the downstream exposure and intermediate composition, but do not identify a rate-limiting step because several variables changed together. Table S16 and Figure S20 report the conditions and apparatus; Tables S17–S18 connect the proposals to implementation changes and component molar feeds. Together with the photochemical case, this experiment shows the role of FlowPilot in formulating testable, connected process choices whose chemical performance remains subject to measurement.

before: Gas equivalents were calculated from the reactive-gas molar flow divided by the limiting-reactant molar flow, including gas composition and the stated reference temperature and pressure. The proposal STP convention was 273.15 K and 1 atm. Where required by a benchmark contract, in-channel gas volume was derived by ideal-gas scaling using absolute operating pressure and temperature. The inlet-reference index V/(Qliquid + Qgas,STP) was kept separate from pressure-corrected nominal time and from measured residence time. Ideal-gas correction alone does not determine liquid holdup or residence-time distribution; a no-slip estimate additionally neglects phase slip, gas dissolution or consumption, and axial pressure variation. Pressure-loss and thermal screening used the selected geometry, phase assumptions, and available material properties; estimated heat-transfer or reaction-enthalpy inputs were identified as assumptions. The implemented quantities, multiphase conventions, and heat-transfer screening are detailed in ESI Section 5 and Table S10.

before: NMR yields were reported using 1,3-benzodioxole as the internal standard. Isolated products were characterized by 1H and 13C NMR spectroscopy and low-resolution mass spectrometry. Shared response-set entries in the supplied laboratory record were treated as grouped operating points, not independent replicates, and no experimental standard deviation was assigned without individual measurements. ESI Section 8 contains the feed preparation, work-up, irradiation specifications, apparatus photographs, and characterization records; Figures S21–S24 reproduce the product spectra. MFC reference-state confirmation, collection windows, and quantitative-NMR calculation records are identified there as outstanding metadata rather than filled by inference.
